1. Introduction

Tintinalli Ch.193 p.1267
  • Cardiac glycosides include digoxin (most common), digitoxin, ouabain, and naturally occurring sources (oleander, foxglove, lily of the valley, toad venom).
  • Indicated for atrial fibrillation rate control and heart failure (declining use due to narrow therapeutic index).
  • Two patterns of toxicity:
    • Acute — intentional or accidental ingestion; younger, no underlying heart disease; presents with hyperkalemia.
    • Chronic — older patients on therapy; impaired renal/heart function; insidious onset; mortality higher than acute.
  • Therapeutic range: 0.5–2 ng/mL for AF rate control / heart failure (lower target now preferred).
  • Toxic threshold: commonly >2 ng/mL but toxicity can occur at therapeutic levels in chronic users with electrolyte abnormalities.

2. Pathophysiology

Tintinalli p.1267

Mechanism of action

  • Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump in cardiac myocytes → ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → reduced Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺ → enhanced contractility (positive inotropy).
  • Vagal effect: increases vagal tone → slows AV node conduction (negative dromotropy) and slows heart rate (negative chronotropy).
  • In overdose: dramatic Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition → severe hyperkalemia (acutely) + delayed afterdepolarizations → triggered automaticity → almost any dysrhythmia.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Absorption: peak 1–3 h after oral ingestion; bioavailability 65–80%.
  • Volume of distribution: very large (~6–7 L/kg) → poorly dialyzable.
  • Distribution: 6 h tissue equilibration — serum levels >6 h post-ingestion are most reliable.
  • Half-life: 36–48 h normally; up to 5+ days in CKD.
  • Excretion: primarily renal; renal failure → toxicity.
Pearl — timing of digoxin level: serum levels obtained before 6 h post-acute-ingestion are misleading because of slow tissue distribution. Wait 6 h for an accurate level (or use 6-h post-ingestion serum level and clinical findings).

3. Sources of Cardiac Glycosides

Tintinalli p.1268
  • Pharmaceutical: digoxin (Lanoxin), digitoxin, lanatoside.
  • Plants:
    • Foxglove (Digitalis purpurea) — original source
    • Oleander (Nerium oleander) — common Mediterranean ornamental; all parts toxic
    • Lily of the valley (Convallaria majalis)
    • Yellow oleander (Thevetia peruviana)
    • Squill / red squill
    • Rhododendron, mountain laurel
  • Animal: Bufo toad (toad venom — Chinese herbal "ChanSu")
  • Cross-reactivity: plant and animal cardiac glycosides cross-react with digoxin immunoassays — Fab can sometimes work for non-digoxin glycoside ingestions.
Pearl — herbal/plant glycoside poisoning: if a patient with no digoxin prescription has a positive digoxin level + cardiac glycoside features → suspect plant ingestion (oleander, toad venom). Digoxin Fab can still be effective.

4. Clinical Features — Acute vs Chronic

Tintinalli Table 193-1 p.1267
📚 Table 193-1 — Clinical Presentation of Digitalis Glycoside Toxicity: Acute vs Chronic (Tintinalli p.1267)
FeatureAcute toxicityChronic toxicity
HistoryIntentional or accidental (single ingestion)Elderly on diuretic; renal insufficiency; drug interaction
GINausea, vomiting, abdominal painLess severe; persistent N/V/anorexia
CNSHeadache, dizziness, confusion, comaFatigue, weakness, confusion, delirium → often misdiagnosed as dementia or stroke
Cardiac (ECG)Bradycardia or supraventricular tachydysrhythmias with AV blockAlmost any dysrhythmia (multiple types simultaneously)
ElectrolytesHyperkalemia (predicts mortality)Normal, decreased, or increased K⁺; hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia common
Digoxin levelMarked elevation (if obtained ≥6 h post-ingestion)May be only minimally elevated or even within "therapeutic" range

"Visual" disturbances

  • Yellow halos around lights (xanthopsia) — classic but uncommon.
  • Snow vision, blurred vision, scotomata.

Atypical presentations

  • Elderly: confusion + non-specific malaise + new arrhythmia → think digoxin.
  • Children: typically pediatric exploratory ingestion → severe but rarely fatal with prompt Fab.
⚠️ Pearl — chronic toxicity is more dangerous than acute: chronic toxicity has higher mortality despite often-LOWER digoxin levels. Toxic effects depend on the patient's overall electrolyte status (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺) more than the absolute drug level.
Inline MCQ 1. Which is the strongest predictor of mortality in ACUTE digoxin toxicity?
A. Patient age
B. Heart rate
C. Hyperkalemia (serum K⁺ >5 mEq/L)
D. Digoxin level alone
Answer: C. Hyperkalemia in acute digoxin toxicity reflects the magnitude of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition — strong mortality predictor. K⁺ >5.5 mEq/L = high mortality without Fab. Reference: Tintinalli Table 193-1.

5. ECG Findings

Tintinalli Fig 193-1 p.1268

Therapeutic ECG changes ("Digitalis effect")

  • "Scooped" or "sagging" ST-segment depression with downsloping
  • Flattened, biphasic, or inverted T-waves
  • Shortened QT interval
  • Increased U-wave amplitude
  • These changes do NOT correlate with toxicity — patients on therapeutic digoxin can show all of these.

Toxic ECG findings — almost any dysrhythmia

  • Bradydysrhythmias: sinus bradycardia, AV blocks (1°, 2°, 3°), junctional rhythm.
  • Tachydysrhythmias: PVCs (most common — bigeminy/trigeminy classic), VT (uncommon), atrial tachycardia with block (PAT with block — pathognomonic).
  • "Combination dysrhythmias": SVT + AV block, atrial fib + slow ventricular response, accelerated junctional rhythm — multiple at once.
  • Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia — pathognomonic but rare; alternating right/left axis QRS.
📚 Fig 193-1 — ECG: A) digoxin level 0.9 ng/mL — scooped ST + small U-waves (therapeutic); B) digoxin level 1.54 — flattening of T waves + first-degree AV block (Tintinalli p.1268)
Pearl — pathognomonic for digitalis toxicity:
• Atrial tachycardia with AV block ("PAT with block") — strongly suggestive of digoxin toxicity.
• Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia — rare but classic.
• Both warrant urgent Fab consideration.
Inline MCQ 2. Which ECG finding is PATHOGNOMONIC for digoxin toxicity?
A. Sinus tachycardia
B. Atrial tachycardia with block (PAT with block) or bidirectional VT
C. RBBB
D. Q waves in inferior leads
Answer: B. Atrial tachycardia with AV block + bidirectional VT are classic for digitalis toxicity. Reference: Tintinalli p.1268.

6. Diagnosis & Laboratory

Tintinalli p.1268

Workup

  • Serum digoxin level — best obtained ≥6 h post-ingestion (allows tissue distribution).
  • BMP — focus on K⁺ (key prognostic), Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, BUN/Cr (renal function).
  • ECG + continuous cardiac monitoring.
  • CBC, LFT.
  • Co-ingestant screen (APAP, salicylate, ETOH).

Interpreting digoxin level

TimeAcuteChronic
<6 h post-ingestionMisleading (still distributing)Reflects steady state
>6 h post-ingestionReliableReliable
"Therapeutic"0.5–2 ng/mL0.5–2 ng/mL
"Toxic">6–10 ng/mL acute>2 ng/mL with symptoms
Indication for Fab≥10 ng/mL or K⁺ >5 mEq/L>6 ng/mL with symptoms (or K⁺ ≥5)

K⁺ thresholds

  • K⁺ <5.0 mEq/L: low mortality risk; Fab not always needed.
  • K⁺ 5.0–5.5: moderate; consider Fab.
  • K⁺ >5.5: high mortality without Fab; Fab indicated.
  • Pre-Fab K⁺ correction: do NOT give calcium IV in suspected digoxin toxicity — historically thought to cause "stone heart" (severe contracture); recent evidence is debated, but widely recommended to avoid.
⚠️ Pearl — calcium in hyperkalemia from digoxin: traditionally CONTRAINDICATED ("stone heart" risk) — though modern evidence is conflicting. Use Fab instead as primary therapy. If hyperkalemia is severe and Fab unavailable: insulin/glucose, kayexalate, dialysis (last resort).

7. Treatment Overview

Tintinalli Table 193-2 p.1269
📚 Table 193-2 — Overview: Treatment of Digitalis Glycoside Poisoning (Tintinalli p.1269)

General principles

  1. ABCs — secure airway, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring.
  2. Stop digoxin; review for drug interactions / nephrotoxic agents.
  3. GI decontamination: activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO if <1 h post-ingestion + airway protected. Multidose AC may help (digoxin has enterohepatic circulation).
  4. Treat hyperkalemia: see above caveats.
  5. Treat dysrhythmias: see below.
  6. Digoxin-specific Fab for life-threatening or refractory toxicity.

Treatment of dysrhythmias

  • Symptomatic bradydysrhythmias:
    • Atropine 0.5–1 mg IV (may help temporarily).
    • Transcutaneous pacing while awaiting Fab — but be aware pacing wires can trigger malignant arrhythmias in digoxin-toxic myocardium.
    • Digoxin Fab definitive.
  • Tachydysrhythmias / VT:
    • Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV — useful for digoxin-induced VT (depletion of Mg²⁺ contributes to toxicity).
    • Lidocaine can be used (has Class IB action without worsening AV block).
    • Phenytoin historically used; less common now.
    • Avoid Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics (procainamide, quinidine, flecainide) — worsen AV block.
    • Avoid β-blockers in bradycardia (worsen AV block).
Avoid in digoxin toxicity:
• Calcium IV for hyperkalemia (debated, but commonly avoided).
• Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics (procainamide, quinidine, flecainide).
• β-blockers for bradydysrhythmias (worsen AV block).
• Cardioversion/defibrillation at higher energy or in rapidly compensating arrhythmias unless absolutely necessary.
Inline MCQ 3. Which IV agent is recommended for digoxin-induced VT?
A. Procainamide
B. Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV (and lidocaine if needed)
C. Adenosine
D. Calcium gluconate
Answer: B. Magnesium sulfate is helpful (K⁺-sparing antiarrhythmic action). Lidocaine for VT without worsening AV block. AVOID Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics. Reference: Tintinalli p.1269.

8. Digoxin-Specific Fab Fragments (DigiFab) — The Antidote

Tintinalli Table 193-3 p.1270
📚 Table 193-3 — Indications for Digoxin-Specific Antibody Fragments (Tintinalli p.1270)

Indications for DigiFab

  1. Life-threatening dysrhythmia: hemodynamically significant bradycardia, AV block (2°/3°), VT, VF.
  2. Hyperkalemia >5 mEq/L in acute digoxin toxicity (high mortality predictor).
  3. Hemodynamic instability: shock, hypotension.
  4. End-organ dysfunction: AKI, AMS attributable to digoxin.
  5. Massive ingestion: >10 mg in adult / >4 mg in child.
  6. Serum digoxin level >15 ng/mL acute, >6 ng/mL chronic with symptoms.
  7. Plant or animal cardiac glycoside ingestion with cardiotoxicity.

DigiFab dosing

ScenarioDose
Cardiac arrest from digoxin toxicity10–20 vials IV bolus
Acute, life-threatening, dose unknown10 vials IV (then repeat 10 if no response)
Chronic toxicity, dose unknown3–6 vials IV
Pediatric, dose unknown1–2 vials IV initially
Calculated by ingested dose:vials = ingested mg × 0.8 (bioavailability) ÷ 0.5 (mg/vial)
Calculated by serum level:vials = level (ng/mL) × weight (kg) ÷ 100

How DigiFab works

  • Ovine-derived antibody fragments (Fab).
  • Binds digoxin in serum + extracts from tissue → restores Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → reverses toxicity.
  • Onset: cardiac signs improve within 30–60 min; complete reversal by 4 h.
  • Bound complex excreted renally — caution in renal failure (use HD if needed).
  • Cross-reacts with plant/animal glycosides — useful for oleander, toad venom, yellow oleander.

After DigiFab

  • Serum digoxin level becomes UNINTERPRETABLE after Fab — total level rises (bound + unbound) but free level drops to zero. Don't redose based on post-Fab levels.
  • K⁺ may drop rapidly — recheck and replace as needed (don't over-correct).
  • Watch for hypersensitivity reaction (rare with modern Fab).
  • Patients in AKI: bound complex excreted slowly → may need HD or repeat Fab.
⚠️ Pearl — Fab in pulseless arrest: for cardiac arrest from suspected digoxin toxicity → empiric 10–20 vials IV bolus during CPR. Don't wait for confirmation.
Inline MCQ 4. Which is an indication for DigiFab in acute digoxin toxicity?
A. Asymptomatic level 1.5 ng/mL
B. Hyperkalemia >5 mEq/L OR life-threatening dysrhythmia OR severe symptoms
C. Hypokalemia
D. Always for any level >1 ng/mL
Answer: B. K⁺ >5 mEq/L acute is a strong mortality predictor; Fab indicated. Also: life-threatening arrhythmia, hemodynamic instability, level >15 ng/mL. Reference: Tintinalli Table 193-3.
Inline MCQ 5. The empiric DigiFab dose for cardiac arrest from suspected digoxin toxicity is:
A. 1 vial IV
B. 5 vials IV
C. 10–20 vials IV bolus
D. 50 vials IV
Answer: C. 10–20 vials IV bolus during CPR for empiric coverage in suspected digoxin arrest. Reference: Tintinalli Table 193-3.

9. Electrolyte Management

Tintinalli p.1269

Hyperkalemia management

  • Best treatment = digoxin Fab (reverses underlying mechanism).
  • If Fab unavailable / awaiting:
    • Insulin + dextrose (10 units regular insulin + 1 amp D50 IV) — shifts K⁺ intracellularly.
    • Sodium bicarbonate (50 mEq IV) — for severe acidosis only.
    • β-agonist nebulizer (albuterol 10–20 mg) — adjunct.
    • Avoid IV calcium — historically thought to cause "stone heart"; modern evidence debated but commonly avoided.
    • Hemodialysis for refractory hyperkalemia — but does NOT remove digoxin (large Vd).
    • Kayexalate can be used but slow.

Hypokalemia (chronic toxicity often)

  • Replace K⁺ aggressively (often deficient from diuretics).
  • Hypokalemia worsens digoxin toxicity (potentiates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition).

Hypomagnesemia

  • Common in chronic digoxin users on diuretics.
  • Replace with magnesium sulfate 2 g IV (esp. for VT).
  • Mg²⁺ is calcium-channel-blocker-like → stabilizes myocardium.

Hypocalcemia / hypercalcemia

  • Hypercalcemia worsens toxicity.
  • Avoid IV calcium (per discussion above).

10. Disposition

Tintinalli p.1270
  • Discharge: rare for any digoxin toxicity; only if asymptomatic + no end-organ effects + low level + reliable disposition + observation 6+ hours.
  • Telemetry: any documented level above therapeutic + symptoms + cardiac monitoring needed.
  • ICU: Fab administration, hemodynamic instability, severe dysrhythmia, refractory hyperkalemia.
  • Transplant referral: rare; intractable cardiogenic shock from chronic toxicity.
  • Psychiatric evaluation for intentional ingestion before discharge.

⚕️ ATLS 11th — Digoxin Toxicity Considerations

ATLS
  • Suspect digoxin toxicity in unconscious elderly trauma patients with arrhythmias and hyperkalemia.
  • Avoid IV calcium for trauma-related hyperkalemia if digoxin toxicity suspected.
  • Empirical DigiFab in cardiac arrest with suspected digitalis toxicity (e.g., elderly + AF on digoxin + new-onset arrhythmia).
  • RSI considerations: rocuronium preferred (avoid succinylcholine if hyperkalemia from digoxin); ketamine acceptable; fentanyl acceptable.
  • Cardiac arrest: standard ACLS + empiric Fab + magnesium + supportive care.

📗 Rosen's EM 10th — Cardiac Glycoside Toxicity

Rosen's Ch.142
  • Same overall framework — K⁺ as key prognostic factor; Fab as definitive therapy.
  • Calcium controversy: Rosen's notes the "stone heart" phenomenon may be exaggerated based on modern data — but recommends caution and Fab as primary therapy.
  • Plant glycosides: Rosen's emphasizes oleander as a common worldwide poison (especially in tropical/subtropical regions); Fab cross-reactivity often allows treatment.
  • Bidirectional VT: Rosen's notes pathognomonic association with digitalis (also seen in catecholaminergic polymorphic VT).
  • Toad venom (Bufo): contains bufadienolides — cardiac glycoside-like; cross-reacts with digoxin assay; Fab works.
  • Refractory cases: ECMO + serial Fab can rescue.
  • Standard "therapeutic" digoxin level has been lowered (0.5–0.9 ng/mL for HF; 1–2 ng/mL for AF rate control) — narrow therapeutic index.

🔑 Key Points (High-Yield)

  1. Mechanism: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition → ↑ intracellular Na⁺ + Ca²⁺ → enhanced contractility + arrhythmogenicity.
  2. Hyperkalemia >5 mEq/L = strong mortality predictor in acute toxicity.
  3. Pathognomonic ECG: atrial tachycardia with AV block (PAT with block) + bidirectional VT.
  4. Vd is large (~6-7 L/kg) — NOT dialyzable.
  5. Serum level ≥6 h post-ingestion for accurate interpretation; pre-6h misleading.
  6. Acute vs Chronic: chronic has HIGHER mortality despite often-lower levels (in elderly with electrolyte derangements).
  7. DigiFab indications: K⁺ >5, life-threatening arrhythmia, severe symptoms, level >15 ng/mL acute / >6 chronic, plant/animal glycoside ingestion.
  8. DigiFab cardiac arrest dose: 10–20 vials IV bolus during CPR.
  9. DigiFab calc: vials = (level × kg) / 100, OR ingested mg × 0.8 / 0.5.
  10. Avoid: IV calcium ("stone heart" risk), Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics, β-blockers in bradycardia.
  11. VT treatment: magnesium 2 g IV + lidocaine; phenytoin historic.
  12. Bradycardia: atropine + transcutaneous pacing (caution); definitive = Fab.
  13. K⁺ management without Fab: insulin/dextrose + bicarb (if acidosis) + albuterol; HD for refractory K⁺ but doesn't remove digoxin.
  14. Plant glycosides (oleander, foxglove, lily of valley, toad venom) — cross-react with digoxin assay AND Fab.
  15. Post-Fab digoxin level is UNINTERPRETABLE — total rises, free near zero. Don't redose based on it.
  16. Multidose AC useful — digoxin has enterohepatic recirculation.
  17. Hypomagnesemia + hypokalemia potentiate toxicity — replace early.
  18. Therapeutic levels do NOT exclude toxicity in chronic users.
  19. Bufo toad venom (ChanSu, Chinese herbal) = cardiac glycoside-like → Fab effective.
  20. "One pill can kill" — pediatric digoxin ingestion of 1–2 mg can be fatal; admit + Fab.
